power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Cancellation tasks are widely used measures of attention but are conventionally scored by metrics such as mean accuracy or concentration scores, disregarding the temporal structure of responding.

Here, we derive two reaction-time (RT) biomarkers from our tablet-based UCancellation task in 388 young adults: intra-individual RT variability (RTV), a marker of sustained attention, and switch cost, an index of cognitive flexibility from transitions between two different task's target categories.
Because consecutive targets are separated by a variable number of scanned distractors, both are confounded by search effort, which we remove with a scanning-load (p) correction framework.

RTV behaved as a scored individual-difference measure: correction improved reliability and convergent validity against TOVA low-frequency RTV (n = 373), and a cross-target composite was the most reliable index.
Switch cost behaved as a within-task phenomenon whose sign reversed with load-large and positive when targets were adjacent, reversing as scanning load increased-consistent with inhibition of return.
Together, these metrics show that RT structure within a brief cancellation task carries attentional information that standard metrics alone does not capture.

Selective attention-focusing on relevant stimuli while suppressing distractors-and sustained attention-maintaining consistent focus over time-are foundational components of cognitive control (Cohen, 2014; Pashler et al., 2001; Sarter et al., 2001).

text.text: Cancellation tasks, such as the d2 Test of Attention, in which participants scan a field of stimuli and mark targets while rejecting distractors, are among the most widely used measures of these abilities, indexing processing speed, concentration, and inhibitory control (Brickenkamp & Zillmer, 1998).

text.text: Our UCancellation task (Pahor et al., 2022), adapts this paradigm to tablets and smartphones and extending its existing set of stimuli, correlating well with the standard paper-and-pencil d2 Test of Attention and providing a brief, engaging, self-administered measure of selective attention and concentration Cancellation performance is traditionally summarized by accuracy-based scores such as concentration performance (hits minus false alarms).

text.text: Yet every response also carries a reaction time (RT), and the temporal structure of responding encodes information about attention and cognitive control that accuracy alone does not capture.
Two RT-derived constructs are especially informative, and neither is used by conventional cancellation scoring.
The first is intra-individual reaction-time variability (RTV), the trial-to-trial fluctuation in response speed.
RTV is among the most robust behavioral markers of sustained attention with greater variability reflecting momentary lapses in attentional control (Machida et al., 2019; Yamashita et al., 2021).

text.text: Elevated RTV is a hallmark of conditions characterized by attentional instability, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (Adams et al., 2011; Castellanos et al., 2005; Kofler et al., 2013), schizophrenia (Kaiser et al., 2008), autism spectrum disorder (Schachar et al., 2023), and Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment (Duchek et al., 2009; Gorus et al., 2008; Tales et al., 2012).

text.text: Extracting RTV from a brief cancellation task could therefore provide a sensitive, low-burden marker of attentional stability.

The second RT-derived biomarker is switch cost, which refers to the additional processing incurred when shifting between task or target sets-a classic index of cognitive flexibility (Wylie & Allport, 2000).

text.text: In the picture version of the UCancellation task, targets alternate between two categories (upright dogs and inverted monkeys), so consecutive target selections can be classified as switches or non-switches.
This allows a switch cost to be estimated within the cancellation task itself, without administering a separate task-switching paradigm.
Deriving these metrics from cancellation data poses a measurement challenge not present in standard RT tasks.

Specifically, consecutive targets are separated by a variable number of intervening distractors that must be scanned, so a response time reflects not only the cognitive process of interest but also search effort.
This scanning load-indexed by the number of items processed since the previous target-confounds both biomarkers and must be removed before RTs can be compared.

text.text: In the design, every ten rows contained exactly forty targets.
Rows were presented for six seconds each, separated by one second blank intervals.
If a participant finished a row before the time limit, they could advance manually to the next trial.
Targets were upright dogs (tail on the left) and upside-down monkeys (tail on the right); all other orientations were non-targets or distractors.
Participants were instructed to select as many targets as possible while avoiding non-targets.
The task consisted of three blocks-two single-target blocks (e.g. only dogs) and one mixed block (dogs and monkeys)-each lasting one minute and ten seconds (see Figure 1 for an illustration).

The present study uses only the mixed block, because it is the sole block in which both target types are present and therefore the only context in which switching between target types can occur.
The traditional UCancellation outcome, Concentration Performance (hits minus false alarms), was retained for reference; our focus is on two novel RT-based biomarkers derived from the same block.

>Correcting Reaction Time for Scanning Load
text.formatted: <head n="2.5." >Correcting Reaction Time for Scanning Load</head>

text.text: RTs following two processed items are not comparable to RTs following four, because the latter entail more visual search; uncorrected, any measure aggregated over p confounds the cognitive effect of interest with search effort.
Scanning load must therefore be controlled for both biomarkers, but the two require different mechanisms because of their structure.
Switch cost, a difference at matched p, has its control built into the matched-p construction, in which the common load cancels; no further model correction is applied.
RTV, a within-category dispersion metric, has no matching to cancel the load and so requires the p-driven trend to be removed explicitly by a correction model.
The two models below are therefore the mechanism by which RTV is corrected.
The ME model treats observed RTV as the sum of a scanning-load component that grows with p and a residual signal, and removes the former.
For each target type, the per-item load slope was estimated as a fixed effect in a linear mixed-effects model with a by-participant random intercept.

For target type c, participant s, and processed-item level p, where 𝛾 0 (𝑐) is the group intercept, 𝛽(𝑐) the per-item load slope, 𝑢 𝑠 (𝑐) the by-participant random intercept (a participant's stable offset in overall RTV), and 𝜀 𝑠,𝑝 (𝑐) the participant-byp residual.
The corrected value subtracts the fitted slope times p, leaving each participant's overall level intact:

The load slope is treated as a stable, construct-irrelevant individual difference and removed once at the group level as a fixed constant; a subtractive form removes only the p-linear trend without rescaling the dispersion, which is the appropriate operation for a variability measure.

ME is a generative model: its slope carries a standard error and supports inference, and-as used below-it can be diagnosed for lack of fit and extended (e.g., with a quadratic term) when the linear form is inadequate.
The PC model assumes RTV grows in proportion to scanned items and normalizes by dividing by p:
PC is a fixed algebraic proportional transform with no estimated parameters.
It provides a simple, parameter-free control and serves as the deployable comparison against ME.
Because it cannot be diagnosed or extended, it cannot adapt when the true load function departs from proportionality-the point at which the two approaches diverge.
Because the linear form is an assumption, we tested it for each target type to determine the appropriate correction.
We compared the linear model against a quadratic model (adding p²) and against a saturated model treating p as categorical (likelihood-ratio tests, maximum-likelihood fits, restricted to p ≤ 4).
Where the linear form was adequate, it was retained.
Where it was not, the sign and size of the departure were examined to decide whether a more complex correction improved the biomarker or merely added noise.
The resulting decisions are reported in Results.

RTV was corrected within each target type using that target type own load slope, because the three types differ in scanning dynamics, a single shared slope would over-correct types whose RTV grows more slowly and under-correct those whose RTV grows more steeply, leaving residual load in some tracks.

Non-switched Targets in particular follow a distinct load function; estimating their slope separately both yields an appropriate correction for the NonSW RTV biomarker and permits a direct test of whether their per-item slope differs from that of the other types.

To evaluate the validity of the UCancellation biomarkers, participants completed the Test of Variables of Attention (TOVA), administered through Inquisit Web; usable data were available for 373 participants.

The TOVA is a continuous performance task and a standard benchmark for sustained attention (Forbes, 1998; Greenberg & Waldman, 1993), from which we took reactiontime variability as the convergent criterion.
text.formatted: The TOVA is a continuous performance task and a standard benchmark for sustained attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Forbes, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Greenberg & Waldman, 1993)</ref>, from which we took reactiontime variability as the convergent criterion.

text.text: In the task, participants are instructed to fixate in the center of the screen while attending to the upper and lower parts of the display.
If the stimulus (small square) appears in the upper part, it is a target and participants must press a key.
Instead, if the stimulus appears in the lower part, it is a non-target, and participants must hold the key press.
The TOVA includes low-frequency (rare-target) and high-frequency (frequent-target) blocks.

We took the low-frequency blocks as the convergent criterion, because RTV is theorized as a marker of vigilance and sustained attention, and low-frequency blocks-with long waits between rare targets-tax vigilance, whereas high-frequency blocks primarily load prepotent responding.
Analyses were conducted in MATLAB 2025b.
Because many measures departed from normality, associations were quantified with Spearman correlations.
Reliability and convergent validity were computed for the RTV biomarkers only; switch cost, a within-task phenomenon, is characterized by its profile across p (above).
Where appropriate we conducted standard likelihood-ratio test and t-tests.

Split-half reliability of each RTV biomarker (the three per-target-type scores and the composite) was estimated as the Spearman correlation between scores computed on the two trial halves (odd vs even trials), 𝜌 ℎℎ , and stepped up to the full test length by the Spearman-Brown formula, 𝜌 full = 2𝜌 ℎℎ /(1 + 𝜌 ℎℎ ).

For the corrected scores, the fixed group slope estimated on the full sample was applied to each half as a constant, rather than refitting the model within each half, so that the reliability estimate reflects the stability of the score and not sampling variability in the slope.

To enable a like-for-like comparison, the reliability of the TOVA low-frequency criterion (its two-block Spearman correlation) is also expressed on the same full-length Spearman-Brown basis, so that UCancellation reliabilities and the criterion's reliability are compared as full-length coefficients.

The association between each RTV biomarker and TOVA low-frequency RTV was estimated as an observed Spearman correlation with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval (5,000 resamples), in the 373-participant subsample.
TOVA is the appropriate convergent criterion for RTV because both index sustained-attention/response consistency.
Observed correlations with their confidence intervals are the primary evidence.

To test whether correcting for scanning load improves the biomarker, ME and PC were each compared against the uncorrected (raw) RTV score-the same collapse over p with no load correction-on split-half reliability and observed convergent validity, for every per-target-type biomarker and the composite.
ME and PC were also compared with each other, and the composite was compared against the strongest single per-type track.
These analyses concern raw RT data.
Per-item RT slopes were compared across target types in a single mixed-effects model with a p × target-type interaction, testing whether the NonSW slope exceeds the FT and SW slopes.
The switch-cost profile across p (≤ 4) was tested for a sign change using per-p tests against zero, the significance of the switch-cost-on-p slope, and the estimated zero-crossing.

In the present study we derived two RT biomarkers from the UCancellation task-reaction-time variability (RTV) and switch cost-and characterized their behaviors as a function of scanning load (p), the number of items processed since the previous target.
Both proved informative, but in different ways and to different evidentiary standards.
RTV behaved as a scored individualdifference measure of sustained attention, showing reliable convergent validity with an established continuous-performance criterion (TOVA).
Switch cost behaved as a within-task phenomenon whose sign reverses with scanning load.
Below we interpret each in turn, then consider the correction framework and the study's limitations.
One interesting behavioral finding was the reversal of switch cost across p.

When targets were adjacent (p = 1), switching to a new target category was substantially slower than maintaining it-the classic switch cost expected from the task-switching literature, in which rearranging resources to a competing and similar task carries a processing penalty (Allport et al., 1994; Los, 1996; Wylie & Allport, 2000).
text.formatted: When targets were adjacent (p = 1), switching to a new target category was substantially slower than maintaining it-the classic switch cost expected from the task-switching literature, in which rearranging resources to a competing and similar task carries a processing penalty <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allport et al., 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Los, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Wylie & Allport, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: As scanning load increased, however, this cost shrank to zero (near p = 2) and then reversed by p = 3 non-switched targets were slower than switched targets.
Decomposing the reversal showed that it arises not from any change in switching per se but from a difference in how steeply reaction time grows with search load across target types.
Specifically, non-switched targets accumulated per-item search cost most rapidly, surpassing switched targets as more items intervened.
Importantly, this steeper growth was approximately linear rather than accelerating, indicating a constant elevated per-item cost rather than a runaway process.
This pattern is consistent with inhibition of return (IOR), the tendency for attention to be discouraged from returning to recently inspected locations or items (Klein, 2000).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with inhibition of return (IOR), the tendency for attention to be discouraged from returning to recently inspected locations or items <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Klein, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Under the foraging-facilitator account, inhibitory tags accumulate on inspected items to bias search forward (Klein & MacInnes, 1999), and such tags have been estimated to persist over roughly four previously inspected items (Wang & Klein, 2010)-the same window over which our reversal appears.
text.formatted: Under the foraging-facilitator account, inhibitory tags accumulate on inspected items to bias search forward <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Klein & MacInnes, 1999)</ref>, and such tags have been estimated to persist over roughly four previously inspected items <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Wang & Klein, 2010)</ref>-the same window over which our reversal appears.

text.text: When a target repeats its category (non-switch), the searcher must continue scanning increasingly tagged and recently rejected items of the same kind, resulting in a increasing per-item penalty.
In contrast, a category switch redirects attention toward a differently coded set that is less subject to accumulated inhibition.
On this reading, the "reverse switch cost" at high p is not a failure of switching but a signature of the inhibitory machinery that makes serial search efficient.

Because a value collapsed across p averages the positive and negative regimes to near zero, the phenomenon is best described by its full p-profile, and the p = 1 value-where switching is isolated from these search dynamics-is the appropriate singlecondition readout for applications.
The non-switched condition was distinctive on both biomarkers, but in different ways.

In mean reaction time it showed the steepest, and essentially linear, growth with load whereas in variability it showed a strongly concave, saturating profile, with most of its individual-difference signal concentrated at low p.

That a single condition is linear in central tendency yet nonlinear in dispersion underscores that RT level and RT variability are separable aspects of performance rather than redundant summaries (Yamashita et al., 2021), and that variability carries dynamics not visible in the mean.
text.formatted: That a single condition is linear in central tendency yet nonlinear in dispersion underscores that RT level and RT variability are separable aspects of performance rather than redundant summaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Yamashita et al., 2021)</ref>, and that variability carries dynamics not visible in the mean.

text.text: RTV is among the most robust behavioural markers of sustained-attention capacity and is elevated across ADHD, ageing, and other conditions marked by attentional lapses (Castellanos et al., 2005; Kofler et al., 2013; Machida et al., 2019).
text.formatted: RTV is among the most robust behavioural markers of sustained-attention capacity and is elevated across ADHD, ageing, and other conditions marked by attentional lapses <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Castellanos et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kofler et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Machida et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Our RTV biomarkers converged with TOVA low-frequency variability, a theoretically matched criterion, with first-target RTV the strongest single correlate.

These correlations were modest in absolute terms but should be read against the psychometric ceiling because the criterion is itself only moderately reliable, the maximum attainable convergent correlation is well below one, and the observed correlations recover a substantial fraction of that ceiling (~ 40%).
A composite across the three target types was the most reliable index-exceeding every single track and the criterion's own reliability-and matched the best single track on validity.

The composite is therefore the more reliable single index for deployment, though not a more valid one; the reliability gain reflects the cancellation of track-specific error through aggregation rather than the addition of new attention-relevant variance.

This strong internal consistency establishes the composite as a promising candidate index, and a natural next step is to characterize its temporal stability, or test-retest reliability, which is the property most relevant to tracking individuals and detecting change over time.

As UCancellation is brief and repeatable, it is well suited to such an evaluation, and benchmarking its across-session stability against that of established continuous-performance measures such as the TOVA would help confirm its utility as a practical alternative.

Removing scanning-load variance is essential before RTV can be compared across trials, and the benefit of doing so was demonstrable by the improved reliability and convergent validity of the RTV biomarkers after correction.

The effect was especially dramatic for non-switched targets, whose steep load dependence rendered the raw score neither reliable nor valid, but which became a usable biomarker once the load trend was removed.
Having established that correcting helps, we contrasted a mixed-effects correction with a simpler per-item transform.
Empirically the two were interchangeable as scores.
That is, convergent validity was statistically indistinguishable, and reliability was comparable across both metrics.

The case for the mixedeffects framework therefore is not based on score superiority but on what it makes possible: it yields interpretable per-target-type slopes whose differences constitute the reaction-time dissociation described above, it can be diagnosed for lack of fit, and it can be extended when its functional assumptions fail-none of which a fixed proportional transform permits.
We therefore adopt the mixed-effects decomposition as the analytic framework while noting that, for pure deployment, the simpler transform yields a near-identical index.
There are several limitations to our current study.
First, the convergent criterion was moderately reliable, capping observable validity and leaving the true convergence underestimated.
Switch cost is reported as a group-level phenomenon rather than a validated individual-difference trait.
Because its sign depends on scanning load, it does not behave as a stable scored measure, and we make no claim about its reliability or its convergent validity.
Non-switched RTV, though a genuine biomarker, was the least reliable track, and its curvature means a linear correction is a deliberate approximation rather than a faithful model of its dynamics.

Finally, the IOR account of the reversal, while consistent with the data and with the known time-course of inhibitory tagging, is an interpretation of an observational pattern; direct tests-for example, manipulating inter-target spacing or probing previously inspected items-would be needed to establish the mechanism.
Extracting reaction-time variability and switch cost from the UCancellation task broadens a brief, engaging cancellation measure into a richer assessment of attentional dynamics.

RTV provides a deployable, criterion-valid index of sustained attention, most reliable as a cross-target composite; switch cost reveals a load-dependent reversal that indexes the inhibitory dynamics of serial search.

Together they illustrate that reaction-time structure within a cancellation task carries information about attention and inhibitory control that traditional measures, such as mean accuracy/concentration scores alone do not capture.
